about: Findings of the Kubernetes scans accepted on purpose, each with its reason (#1438; Trivy since #1453). check-scans.js fails on any other finding, and on an entry here that no longer matches anything. Kubescape: control + resources ([file:]Kind/namespace/name, * for any part). kube-bench: check number. Trivy: check + what it covers (file, file:Kind/name, Kind/name, * for any part).

kubescape.reason: OpenShift chooses the uid and group itself (its restricted SCC); a fixed one would be refused there. The Kubernetes and k3s overlays name the image's (1000:1000).
Both talk to the Kubernetes API by design: the dispatcher makes and removes the run Jobs and Secrets in oscar-runs, Alloy reads the oscar pods' logs. Every other pod of OSCAR mounts no token.
The same two accounts as C-0034, for the same reason: their tokens are what lets them do their work, each limited to one namespace by a Role.

The dispatcher removes the Jobs and Secrets it made when their run ends, or when it starts again after losing runs (Secrets by label, in one call), in oscar-runs only (a Role, not a ClusterRole). It never lists nor reads a Secret.

kube-bench.reason: The benchmark reads the first start of the API server in k3s's log. A k3s moved from SQLite to etcd as the guide does (k3s guide, section 9; the CI does the same) first started without etcd. On etcd k3s sets both arguments: the CI checks that the latest start names them.

k3s's own pods (CoreDNS, Traefik, metrics-server, the volume provisioner) need their tokens, and k3s writes their manifests. OSCAR's pods are Kubescape's C-0034 to check, where only the dispatcher and Alloy mount one.

trivy.reason: The platform checks health, not the image: Docker Compose on the VPS (healthcheck of oscar and oscar-runner), probes on Kubernetes (Docker's HEALTHCHECK is ignored there). The run image runs one scenario and ends.

OSCAR's containers run as the user of their image, 1000:1000, which owns the data volume (the Kubernetes and k3s overlays name it, runAsNonRoot is set); a uid above 10000 would change who owns an installed data volume. Alloy runs as its image's own user. OpenShift chooses a high uid itself.

OSCAR's containers run as the user of their image, 1000:1000, which owns the data volume (the Kubernetes and k3s overlays name it, runAsNonRoot is set); a uid above 10000 would change who owns an installed data volume. Alloy runs as its image's own user. OpenShift chooses a high uid itself.

A HelmChart is a k3s object read by k3s's own Helm controller, which takes it from kube-system as k3s's documentation places it; the chart itself installs into the monitoring namespace (targetNamespace).

The runs' namespace has its quota (runs/quota.yaml), which bounds what the dispatcher may start. OSCAR's namespace holds one server pod (replicas 1) and the dispatcher, each with its requests and limits; the monitoring's pods have theirs. Trivy asks for a quota in every file it reads.
The dispatcher makes and removes the run Jobs it starts, in oscar-runs only (a Role, not a ClusterRole): its work. Kubescape's C-0007 is accepted for the same right.

The dispatcher makes each run's Secret, gives it to the run's Job and removes it, in oscar-runs only; it can neither list nor read Secrets (#1438). Kubescape's C-0034/C-0053 are accepted for the same account.

The overlays name no namespace: an operator applies them with -n (oscar in the guides; on OpenShift the project the cluster gives). The CI renders them without one, which Trivy reads as the default namespace.

Trivy guesses from names (PORT, RUN_POD_USER, RUN_TIMEOUT_MS): these ConfigMaps hold ports, times, a uid and addresses, no secret. Every secret is in a Secret (oscar-secrets, oscar-runner), never in a ConfigMap.

Trivy's list of trusted registries leaves out ghcr.io and docker.io. OSCAR's images are those of its own releases on GHCR; every third-party image is pinned by its digest, and the weekly scan (scan-images.yml) reads them all.
